steps.description: Engineering Executive: First 90 Days. The first quarter is a learning quarter — every step below follows from these five principles.

steps.name: Communicate that you will prioritize learning over early change
steps.description: Early changes made without context are usually wrong; the first quarter's output is understanding.

steps.name: Understand systems before modifying them
steps.description: Every system encodes history; what looks broken often solves a problem you cannot see yet.

steps.name: Communicate that you will focus on durable improvements, not visible quick wins
steps.description: Quick wins impress briefly; durable improvements still matter a year later.

steps.name: Build trust before conflict
steps.description: You will need to spend trust on hard calls later; bank it before drawing on it.

steps.name: Move slower than your instincts tell you
steps.description: New executives almost always overestimate what they understand; deliberate pace prevents unforced errors.

links.name: hidden blocker
links.description: I can't say no (pressure of CEO and peers to make fast changes);

steps.description: Week 1–2.

steps.name: Ask your manager to write explicit expectations for your role
steps.description: Written expectations expose misalignment now, not at your first review.

steps.name: Ask: "What will success look like in 6–12 months?"
steps.description: The answer tells you what your manager actually values, beyond the job description.

steps.name: Identify any urgent, dire issues needing immediate attention
steps.description: The learning quarter has exceptions; genuine fires must be found and triaged in week one.

steps.name: Align on measurable goals for your first 90 days
steps.description: Agreed goals protect your learning period from shifting expectations.

steps.name: Understand how the business makes money
steps.description: Every engineering priority call eventually traces back to the revenue model.

steps.name: Know where money is spent and the current financial runway
steps.description: Runway determines how much patience the company can afford for long-term work.

steps.name: Identify what must be true in 12 months for step-function growth
steps.description: This tells you where engineering leverage matters most.

steps.name: Identify knowledge gaps between Engineering and the business
steps.description: Where engineers do not understand the business, effort silently drifts away from impact.

steps.name: Learn the company's core domain deeply
steps.description: Domain fluency is what turns you from a service provider into a strategic peer.

steps.name: Go on a listening tour
steps.description: Meet individuals and teams before forming opinions; people remember who listened first.

steps.name: Meet cross-functional peers and stakeholders
steps.description: Their view of Engineering is data you cannot get from inside the org.

tools.name: Working with Your CEO, Peers, and Engineering
Working with Your CEO, Peers, and Engineering

steps.name: Set up recurring 1:1s
steps.description: With directs and skip-levels; the recurring slot matters more than any single agenda.

steps.name: Share weekly or monthly updates on what you're learning
steps.description: Sharing what you are learning builds trust while making no premature commitments.

steps.name: Attend routine forums before changing them
steps.description: You cannot judge a meeting's value from its description; sit in it first.

steps.name: Shadow support tickets
steps.description: Support tickets show the product's real failure modes, unfiltered.

steps.name: Shadow customer/partner meetings
steps.description: Hearing customers directly beats every internal summary of what customers want.

steps.name: Observe user testing sessions
steps.description: Watching real users struggle recalibrates what 'working software' means.

steps.name: Map how ideas become shipped work
steps.description: The gap between the official process and the real one is where problems hide.

steps.name: Understand how work is assigned and prioritized
steps.description: Whoever actually sets priorities holds power the org chart may not show.

steps.name: Identify who handles emergencies
steps.description: Emergency paths reveal your true key people — and your bus-factor risks.

steps.name: Determine whether execution systems are working and scaling
steps.description: Systems that barely cope today will break at the next doubling.

steps.name: Identify internal Engineering velocity metrics
steps.description: You need a baseline before you can claim — or measure — any improvement.

steps.name: Identify external/business impact metrics
steps.description: Velocity means nothing if it is not moving a business number.

steps.name: Assess team morale and inclusion
steps.description: Morale problems compound quietly and surface as regretted attrition.

steps.name: Identify who is succeeding and who isn't — and why
steps.description: The 'why' distinguishes individual issues from broken systems around people.

steps.name: Document undocumented processes
steps.description: Writing down tribal knowledge tests whether it is real — and protects against departures.

steps.name: Spot-check compensation and inclusion health
steps.description: Compensation inequities are cheapest to fix before they become attrition or legal risk.

steps.name: Pay attention to non-product engineering roles
steps.description: These roles hold the org together but are easy to overlook from the top.

steps.name: Evaluate whether the existing tech stack is effective
steps.description: Judge the stack against the business's needs, not your personal preferences.

steps.name: Identify major friction points
steps.description: Daily friction costs more than dramatic incidents; engineers know where it is — ask.

steps.name: Learn how major technical decisions are made
steps.description: Decision paths show whether architecture is designed or accreted.

steps.name: Build and deploy a small, trivial change yourself
steps.description: Nothing reveals the developer experience like living it once.

steps.name: Join an on-call rotation
steps.description: On-call shows the system's real reliability and the toll it takes on people.

steps.name: Attend incident reviews
steps.description: Incident reviews expose both system weaknesses and the culture around failure.

steps.name: Document the technology history and context behind decisions
steps.description: Today's odd architecture is usually yesterday's rational trade-off; know it before judging.

steps.name: Document the implicit Engineering strategy
steps.description: The org already has a strategy in its actions; writing it down is the first step to changing it.

steps.name: Review hiring funnel metrics and pipeline
steps.description: The funnel shows whether your problem is sourcing, evaluation, or closing.

steps.name: Establish a recurring recruiting meeting
steps.description: A standing rhythm keeps hiring moving without your constant attention.

steps.name: Shadow interviews and onboarding
steps.description: Seeing the candidate experience firsthand shows the bar and brand you actually project.

steps.name: Identify 1–3 highest-priority missing roles
steps.description: A short list focuses recruiting capacity where it changes the org's trajectory.

steps.name: Personally help close top candidates
steps.description: For key candidates, an executive call is often what tips the decision.

steps.name: Evaluate whether the hiring process needs an overhaul
steps.description: Decide deliberately whether to fix or rebuild before hiring scales further.

steps.name: Kick off Engineering brand efforts
steps.description: Brand work takes months to pay off, so the seeds go in early.

steps.name: Limit early changes to 1–2 high-leverage improvements
steps.description: Few and finished beats many and abandoned — every change spends scarce trust.

steps.name: Avoid disrupting systems without a working alternative
steps.description: A flawed working system still beats a better one that does not exist yet.

steps.name: Consider adding a weekly operational review
steps.description: One high-leverage change most orgs lack: a regular look at the numbers together.

steps.name: Evaluate org structure for execution impediments
steps.description: Note structural problems now; reorganize only once you understand the people.

steps.name: Plan next year's org growth
steps.description: Growth planned early avoids reactive hiring and rushed promotions later.

steps.name: Follow a "20–40 rule" for problem-solving before asking for help
steps.description: Wrestling with problems yourself builds context; asking after a set time caps the waste.

steps.name: Create a regular thinking space to slow down
steps.description: Unscheduled thinking time is where scattered observations become judgment.

steps.name: Avoid rushing to judgment without context
steps.description: First impressions in a new org are hypotheses to test, not conclusions.

steps.name: Avoid referencing "how we did it at my last job"
steps.description: The phrase erodes credibility even when the idea is right; translate, do not cite.

steps.name: Write down what you're learning
steps.description: Writing exposes gaps in your understanding and becomes your strategy's raw material.

steps.name: Build a peer support group of similar leaders
steps.description: Some problems can only be discussed with peers outside your company.

steps.name: Consider engaging an executive coach
steps.description: A coach provides the candid, disinterested feedback your org cannot give you.

steps.name: Create space for self-care
steps.description: The role is a marathon; recovery capacity is part of the job.

steps.name: Assess whether team pace is sustainable
steps.description: A pace that needs heroics is not a pace; it is a countdown to attrition.

steps.name: Identify energy drains
steps.description: Naming the drains is the prerequisite to removing them.

steps.name: Add energizing practices deliberately
steps.description: Energy is managed by design, not by waiting for a quieter quarter.

steps.name: Avoid burnout cycles early
steps.description: Burnout patterns set in the first months tend to become the permanent culture.
Engineering Executive: Months 4–12. Convert the diagnosis from your first quarter into strategy, systems, and a team you trust — every step below follows from these principles.

steps.name: Convert your 90-day diagnosis into a written strategy
steps.description: Your first-quarter learning only pays off once it becomes explicit direction others can act on.

steps.name: Build key operating systems that run without you in the room
steps.description: Hiring, planning, and meetings should work through owners and cadences, not your constant presence.

steps.name: Limit concurrent major initiatives — finish and prove value before starting more
steps.description: A few completed, visible wins build more trust than many half-finished changes.

steps.name: Separate decisions: financial plan first, then allocation, then roadmap
steps.description: Debating everything at once creates chaos; sequencing keeps each debate small and resolvable.

steps.name: Keep durable constraints steady; change narrowly and intentionally
steps.description: Stable budgets and allocations let teams plan; when change is needed, change one thing with a stated reason.
Months 4–6.

steps.name: Write the strategy document yourself
steps.description: Delegating the writing signals delegated ownership; the diagnosis and trade-offs must be yours.

steps.name: Build the diagnosis from the roadmap, financials, and survey data; validate it with skeptics
steps.description: A strategy built on a wrong diagnosis fails no matter how good the policies are.

steps.name: Document resource allocation, fundamental rules, and decision rights explicitly
steps.description: These three policy areas decide most day-to-day conflicts before they reach you.

steps.name: Test every policy against three checks
steps.description: A policy that fails any of the three checks is a slogan, not a strategy.

steps.name: Iterate drafts with a working group of 3–5 trusted stakeholders before socializing widely
steps.description: Early private iteration surfaces flaws cheaply and creates allies for the launch.

steps.name: Launch with a ~1-week feedback window; review impact after ~2 months; refresh annually
steps.description: A defined feedback and review rhythm keeps the strategy alive instead of shelfware.

steps.name: If company strategy is undocumented, write down your best understanding of it
steps.description: Engineering strategy must anchor to something; even an informal summary beats guessing.
Aligned with the fiscal-year cycle.

steps.name: Run planning as three separated phases
steps.description: Each phase settles constraints for the next, keeping debates small and decisions durable.

steps.name: Segment costs into headcount, production, and development
steps.description: Different cost types grow for different reasons and need different levers.

steps.name: Model the org structure before requesting headcount; check the plan against recruiting capacity
steps.description: Headcount you can't recruit or absorb is a plan on paper only.

steps.name: Set steady allocation percentages and keep them stable
steps.description: Steady allocation lets teams commit; constant rebalancing destroys momentum.

steps.name: Reserve a fixed validation budget for exploratory work
steps.description: Unscoped ideas need a protected lane; never compare their raw potential against scoped work.

steps.name: Agree the roadmap in open sessions with Product and Design — outcomes first, projects second
steps.description: Open sessions prevent 1:1 side deals; outcome framing leaves teams room to solve.

steps.name: List vendor renewal deadlines for the year; check usage vs. contract before each negotiation
steps.description: Leverage in vendor negotiations comes from time and usage data, not urgency.

steps.name: Run one measurement initiative at a time; start with metrics that feed real decisions
steps.description: Small, useful wins build trust in data; a big measurement program invites resistance.

steps.name: Stand up operational metrics
steps.how: incidents, downtime, latency, cost per business metric
steps.description: These are the health signals customers and the board will ask about first.

steps.name: Instrument delivery lead time and deployment frequency; survey developer experience
steps.description: System metrics show throughput; survey data shows the friction behind it.

steps.name: Set an explicit rule with managers: optimization metrics improve systems, never rate individuals
steps.description: The moment metrics judge people, people start gaming the metrics.

steps.name: Agree one clear goal with the CEO and board, tied to business strategy, and report against it
steps.description: One legible goal beats a dashboard of engineering internals nobody upstairs can parse.

steps.name: Review the data weekly; compare month-over-month and quarter-over-quarter trends
steps.description: Regular review builds intuition for what is normal, so anomalies stand out early.

steps.name: Decide who is on the long-term team; make personnel changes quickly
steps.description: Slow personnel decisions freeze team dynamics; clarity resets them.

steps.name: Write down how the team decides, disagrees, and escalates; call out violations immediately
steps.description: Values only exist if defection is refereed consistently — for everyone.

steps.name: Establish team rituals
steps.how: weekly leadership meeting, update cadence, escalation paths
steps.description: Predictable structure carries information and decisions without depending on heroics.

steps.name: Set explicit expectations: every leader builds a strong team and works peer-to-peer, not in silos
steps.description: You are building leaders of leaders; escalated peer conflicts should be exceptions.

steps.name: Write a personal README covering your working style and decision philosophy
steps.description: The team wastes months guessing how to work with you; write it down instead.

steps.name: Address signs of peer competition in 1:1s before they harden
steps.description: Competition for scope turns a leadership team zero-sum; name it early.

steps.name: Require a written document — not slides — for every recurring review meeting
steps.description: Documents force clear thinking and let the meeting be discussion, not presentation.

steps.name: Schedule the weekly core: leadership meeting, tech spec review, incident review
steps.description: These three carry execution, technical quality, and learning from failure.

steps.name: Add the monthly forums: managers meeting, Staff+ meeting, org-wide Q&A
steps.description: Monthly forums develop leaders and give everyone direct access to you.

steps.name: Hold weekly 1:1s with directs; cap skip-levels at a fixed time budget
steps.description: 1:1s are the primary support channel; the cap keeps skip-levels from crowding out core work.

steps.name: Assign an owner to every recurring meeting; cancel any that stop adding value
steps.description: Ownerless meetings decay into ritual; each should survive a 'would we cancel this?' test.

steps.name: Send a short, predictable update to the org even in quiet weeks
steps.description: The steady drip builds trust and makes big announcements land in context.

steps.name: Package every big announcement
steps.how: tl;dr, who is affected, actions, dates, canonical source
steps.description: A standard packet ensures nobody misses what changed, who is affected, and what to do.

steps.name: Have a trusted reviewer read significant messages before you broadcast them
steps.description: A reviewer catches confusing wording, unintended tone, and missing context cheaply.

steps.name: Repeat major messages across every channel
steps.description: Nobody reads every channel; repetition is how a message actually reaches the org.

steps.name: Before replying to executive feedback, restate the underlying concern and confirm you got it right
steps.description: Feedback often carries a deeper worry — speed, risk, priority; answer that, not the surface detail.

steps.name: Document hiring loops, interview rubrics, and a written leveling framework
steps.description: Documentation turns hiring from personal heroics into a system others can run.

steps.name: Standardize compensation with clear in-band / out-of-band approval rules
steps.description: Consistent offers protect fairness and stop every negotiation escalating to you.

steps.name: Review monthly metrics
steps.how: hires per recruiter, time to hire, offer and acceptance rates
steps.description: A monthly look at the funnel shows where the machine is jammed before quarters are lost.

steps.name: Keep time-to-offer within ~2 weeks; require a high bar for adding interview steps
steps.description: Speed wins candidates; every added step costs more than the signal it usually adds.

steps.name: Join sell calls to personally help close senior and strategic candidates
steps.description: Executive attention is often the deciding factor for senior hires.

steps.name: Train hiring managers; set decision deadlines and intervene on unicorn requirements
steps.description: Most hiring failures are manager behaviors — indecision, impossible requirements — not pipeline problems.

steps.name: Appoint an onboarding orchestrator with real time allocated
steps.description: Without a named owner with real hours, onboarding decays into a slide deck.

steps.name: Start with three sessions: values & strategy, architecture overview, dev-environment setup
steps.description: The worst programs come from trying too hard; start simple and practical.

steps.name: Give every new hire a buddy and a personalized team-level plan
steps.description: Daily buddy check-ins in the first weeks catch friction the manager never sees.

steps.name: Measure time-to-productivity and satisfaction; survey new hires after 1 month
steps.description: Fresh hires see your org's gaps most clearly — capture that before it fades.

steps.name: Review results and iterate quarterly; scale the investment to your hiring rate
steps.description: A structured program pays off around 5–10 hires/month; below that, keep it lightweight.

steps.name: Test every proposed value: reversible, applicable, honest
steps.description: A good value is a real choice another company could invert, usable in trade-offs, and true today.

steps.name: Drop values that describe aspiration, not today's behavior — change behavior first, then write it down
steps.description: Aspirational values read as hypocrisy; documented reality builds credibility.

steps.name: Pilot values with small groups, then integrate them into hiring, promotions, and 1:1s
steps.description: Values that never appear in decisions and promotions are just posters.

steps.name: List where your personal standards exceed what the org supports; pick the few gaps worth the fight
steps.description: Silently compensating for standards nobody shares is the fast path to burnout.

steps.name: Spread higher standards in three steps
steps.how: model one practice visibly → document it → offer it to teams
steps.description: Role modeling spreads standards further than mandates — and shows which teams opt in.

steps.name: Rate each peer relationship — supported, tolerated, or resented — and book 1:1s where it isn't “supported”
steps.description: You cannot succeed while merely tolerated; name the weak relationships and work them.

steps.name: When a peer criticizes Engineering, verify the claim with your team before acting on it
steps.description: Criticism is often a symptom of a broader issue; fix the root cause, not the accusation.

steps.name: When functions clash, write down each side's view and propose one company-first synthesis
steps.description: The integrating narrative is usually yours to write; function-first framing loses allies.

steps.name: After exec meetings, ask one peer: “what could I have done better?”
steps.description: Small, specific feedback requests build the alignment habit and show visible improvement.

steps.name: Resolve stuck disagreements with structured escalation
steps.description: A time-boxed process converts endless re-litigating into a decision everyone commits to.

steps.name: Filter major decisions with: “what maximizes company impact over the next 3 years?”
steps.description: The long-horizon test separates company-first calls from turf defense.
Engineering Executive: Year 2 and beyond. Shift from building systems to inspecting and evolving them — durable disciplines rather than one-off projects.

steps.name: Shift from building systems to inspecting and evolving them
steps.description: Year two's risk is not missing systems — it is systems quietly degrading unobserved.

steps.name: Judge process and judgment quality, not just outcomes
steps.description: Outcomes are noisy; rewarding lucky bets teaches bad decision-making.

steps.name: Commit to operating models for years; change intentionally, not reactively
steps.description: Organizations absorb change slowly; fads cost more than imperfect but stable models.

steps.name: Invest in assets that compound: trust, people, network, reputation
steps.description: These assets take years to build and pay off precisely when you need them most.

steps.name: Protect your energy — this is a decade game, not a quarter game
steps.description: Sustained impact requires a work mix you can sustain, not maximum output.

steps.name: For every delegated area, define how you will independently verify progress
steps.description: Delegation without verification is not trust — it is abdication.

steps.name: Evaluate decisions on process quality, separately from outcomes — reward good process after bad outcomes
steps.description: Punishing good errors and rewarding bad successes optimizes for luck.

steps.name: Run weekly or monthly metric forums; don't rely on quarterly-only reviews
steps.description: Quarterly-only reviews find problems a quarter late.

steps.name: When a concern surfaces, go directly to the people doing the work
steps.description: Summarized narratives filter out exactly the context you need.

steps.name: Chase down confusing reports or metrics immediately — persistent confusion is a trust risk
steps.description: Ambiguity compounds; what confuses you today misleads decisions tomorrow.

steps.name: Invite others to inspect your own work; run a quarterly self-check on where you rely on trust alone
steps.description: Reciprocal inspection proves it is support, not suspicion.

steps.name: Use policy for recurring decisions that need consistency
steps.description: Written policy lets the organization move without you in the room.

steps.name: Use consensus when context is distributed and buy-in matters
steps.description: When no one holds the full picture, the process of being heard is part of the answer.

steps.name: Use conviction for high-stakes, divisive, or stalled decisions
steps.description: Sometimes the org needs a decision more than it needs agreement.

steps.name: Once a month, handle one real decision with your weakest style and debrief it
steps.description: Fluency in all three styles is built by deliberate practice, not preference.

steps.name: Once a quarter, check whether you default to one style out of habit
steps.description: Company context shifts — growth, downturn, scale — and your default should shift with it.

steps.name: Identify which process-ownership pattern you run today
steps.description: You cannot evolve a model you have not named.

steps.name: Before adding process roles, fix execution within the current pattern
steps.description: Most 'we need a TPM org' moments are really under-execution of the baseline.

steps.name: Rotate process ownership and tie it to promotion criteria
steps.description: Rotation prevents burnout and makes process work career-relevant instead of a tax.

steps.name: Run a budget reality check before moving up the cost curve — only do it during growth
steps.description: Specialized roles are hard to fund and harder to unwind in a downturn.

steps.name: Commit to the chosen model for 3–4 years; write down the beliefs behind it
steps.description: Documented beliefs are the antidote to process fads.

steps.name: Design team boundaries and target architecture together
steps.description: Your org chart will ship itself; design boundaries to produce the architecture you want.

steps.name: Classify every team as stream-aligned, platform, enabling, or complicated-subsystem
steps.description: Vague 'support' or 'ops' teams accumulate work no one designed them for.

steps.name: Size teams for cognitive load
steps.how: 5–9 people, one complex domain per team
steps.description: A team owning more than it can understand slows down every domain it touches.

steps.name: Write down every team-to-team interaction mode; time-box collaboration, then move to X-as-a-Service
steps.description: Unbounded collaboration is a smell; stable boundaries should become services.

steps.name: Diagnose each team's state and apply the matching fix
steps.how: falling behind → add people; treading water → cut WIP; repaying debt → add time; innovating → keep slack
steps.description: Each state needs a different intervention; adding people is right for only one of them.

steps.name: Reorganize only for structural problems, and only with a gapless ownership map
steps.description: Reorgs are expensive; run one only when process and culture levers cannot fix it.

steps.name: Refresh succession plans yearly; review team boundaries every few months
steps.description: Boundaries and key-person risk drift silently; regular review catches both.

steps.name: Align with the CEO on what the new executive's 90-day success looks like
steps.description: Shared success criteria prevent the new peer being judged by shifting expectations.

steps.name: Transfer your mental map in their first 2 weeks
steps.how: data, urgent problems, power map, culture
steps.description: Your context — where data lives, who really influences what — saves them months.

steps.name: Each write the other's role expectations independently, then compare and reconcile
steps.description: Accidental role misalignment surfaces now, instead of in a conflict later.

steps.name: Agree conflict handling and an escalation path before you need them
steps.description: Rules agreed in peacetime hold up under pressure.

steps.name: Hold a weekly structured 1:1 plus regular non-transactional time
steps.description: Deep working sessions plus real rapport make peer partnerships durable.

steps.name: Give candid feedback in the first 3–6 months, before missteps compound
steps.description: Mediocre-but-pleasant executives can linger for years; early candor is the kindness.

steps.name: Run the need check first: can you hire senior people and start the interviews you want?
steps.description: If opportunities already flow, minimal investment is the right amount.

steps.name: Pick one timeless topic grounded in real experience; expect to discard 2–3 drafts
steps.description: One deep, durable piece outperforms a stream of shallow content.

steps.name: Publish as a blog post or conference talk; ask 5–10 peers to share it
steps.description: Small formats iterate fast and leave a permanent, discoverable artifact.

steps.name: Host everything on a personal site linked from your profiles
steps.description: Prestige works through easy discoverability when someone looks you up.

steps.name: Timebox the effort; judge it by mentions in interviews and inbound opportunities, not pageviews
steps.description: Followers and traffic are vanity here; the goal is quiet familiarity among people who matter.

steps.name: Showcase the org's most interesting engineering problems in occasional thoughtful content
steps.description: Organizational prestige compounds hiring; meaningful problems attract senior people.

steps.name: Meet ~1 new person per month; keep a simple list and follow up periodically
steps.description: A modest steady rhythm compounds into a real network; bursts do not.

steps.name: After receiving help, close the loop: report back what you did and what worked
steps.description: Closing the loop is what turns a favor into a relationship.

steps.name: Use the network for what it's best at
steps.how: benchmarks, vendor pricing, sensitive advice, backchannels
steps.description: Some questions — compensation, org sizing, backchannels — can only be answered peer-to-peer.

steps.name: Keep cold outreach to 2–4 sentences with one specific question
steps.description: Specific, answerable asks get replies; 'can we chat?' does not.

steps.name: Run or join a small curated peer circle with a code of conduct
steps.description: Sensitive executive topics need small, private, high-trust rooms.

steps.name: Build recruiter, founder, and VC relationships before you need them
steps.description: A network built during a job search is too late; build it from strength.

steps.name: Write the M&A strategy with the executive team before any deal appears
steps.description: Deal pressure is the worst time to decide what kinds of deals make sense.

steps.name: For each deal, write the thesis: what must be true for it to make sense
steps.description: Explicit assumptions give due diligence something to confirm or kill.

steps.name: Run the engineering evaluation across seven areas
steps.how: implementation, IP, security, compliance, integration, costs, culture
steps.description: Read actual source code and audit reports; what you are buying is rarely what is pitched.

steps.name: Write the integration plan before closing
steps.description: Integration cost decides whether the thesis holds; plan it before the price is set.

steps.name: Apply the final test: “would I still approve if I had to personally run the integration?”
steps.description: If the answer is no, the deal's real costs are being carried by someone else on paper.

steps.name: List what energizes you — and ask each of your leaders to do the same
steps.description: You cannot manage a mix you have not named.

steps.name: Schedule some energizing work into everyone's mix
steps.how: small and orthogonal — never opposed to company goals
steps.description: Energizing work is fuel, not indulgence — as long as it never works against company goals.

steps.name: Run a weekly reflection: what energized me, what drained me, is this sustainable for 12+ months?
steps.description: Five minutes weekly catches burnout trends months before they become crises.

steps.name: Sanity-check gray-area side work with a trusted peer
steps.description: Uncertainty about whether work is aligned is itself the warning sign.

steps.name: If imbalance persists for ~a year, change your work mix, role, or environment
steps.description: Chronic depletion does not self-correct; a year is the threshold for acting.
